paras: The attempted lynching of Alex Umphreys was an attack on a Black prisoner by his fellow inmates in the county jail at Columbus, Ohio, on May 16, 1888, after he was jailed on a charge of assaulting a young girl. Inmates nearly drowned him and hoisted him from the floor by a rope around his neck, but he survived. A wire dispatch saying that "Judge Lynch" had come close to ending his life ran in papers from Washington to Texas and Kansas over the following ten days.

Umphreys, described in the dispatches as "a negro," was arrested on a charge of assault upon a little girl and bound over to court. A longer Columbus report gave his name as Alex. Umphreys and said he was charged with the rape of Stella Couch, a nine-year-old white girl, whom the Washington Critic called "the little Crouch girl." That report also asserted, alone among the accounts, that he had "shamelessly acknowledged to the mayor" the offense. Unable to give $1,000 bail, he was taken to the county jail on Wednesday morning.

According to the fuller account, when the other prisoners learned who he was, they surrounded him and announced that they had decided to kill him. They gave him until two o'clock to prepare for death and ordered him to pray over a Bible; he said he could not pray and read a chapter instead. He was then dragged to the bath tub, told he must be washed before he died, and held under the water until he was nearly smothered. Standing before a stove afterward, he was pelted with eggs.

Next they put a bed-cord noose over his head, and three of them ran with the loose end around the corridor. The rope was thrown over an iron beam and he was pulled up off the floor. The wire said one of the prisoners cut the rope before the jail officers arrived; the fuller account credited "one or two of the less excited" prisoners with stepping in. By the fuller account the men then stripped him and scrubbed him in the tub with soft soap and a broom while he pleaded, "For God's sake, don't murder me!"
The Washington Critic's version added that jail officials then appeared and rescued Umphreys. No report of charges against the prisoners, or of the outcome of his case, appears in the coverage.

Most papers carried the story as a short Columbus dispatch dated May 17, which opened, "Judge Lynch came very near making an end of Umphreys," and called him "the brute." It ran on May 17 in the Washington Evening Star, the Alexandria Gazette and the San Antonio Daily Light, and on May 18 in the New York Sun, the Indianapolis Journal and the Fort Worth Daily Gazette. Weeklies, among them the Emporia Weekly News and the Clarke Courier of Berryville, Virginia, followed on May 24, and the Diamond Drill of Crystal Falls, Michigan, on May 26.

Headlines ranged from the plain "Almost Lynched in Jail" and "A Narrow Escape" to the San Antonio Daily Light's "Too Much Mercy for Him" and the Washington Critic's "Tender-Hearted Jail Birds." The New York Sun changed "the brute" to "the man."

The longer account, printed in the Maysville, Kentucky, Evening Bulletin on May 18 and the Logan Ohio Democrat on May 26, named the girl and described the ordeal in detail. It called Umphreys "the colored brute" and "the wretch" and treated the charge as proven, with the Bulletin's headline reading "A Negro Rapist's Narrow Escape." The Ohio Democrat headed it "Rough Usage" and called the attackers "Indignant Prisoners," though the text called Umphreys "the victim" and quoted his pleas.

The wire said a prisoner cut the rope before officers arrived, the Critic that officials then rescued him, and the fuller account that other prisoners intervened and the abuse resumed. The May 17 dispatch said he was arrested "yesterday," while the fuller account placed the arrest on Tuesday and the jailing on Wednesday morning. The girl's surname appears as Couch in the fuller account and as Crouch in the Critic.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Alex Umphreys
bases: Fellow prisoners in the Columbus jail announced they would kill Umphreys, an accused man, and hoisted him from the floor by a rope around his neck, which the papers called a near lynching; he survived, so this is an attempted lynching (A1, A7, A13).

A group of prisoners (at least three hauled the rope) acted without authority to punish Umphreys for the charged assault on a girl, but he was cut down or rescued alive, so no one was killed (A1, A4, A7).
The short Columbus wire (A1, A4) and a separate, longer Columbus account (A7, A13) agree that fellow prisoners ducked him in a bath tub and drew him up by a rope around his neck.

accounts.label: Fuller Columbus account
accounts.gist: Prisoners announced they would kill him, set a two o'clock deadline, made him read the Bible, ducked him, pelted him with eggs and hoisted him over an iron beam until 'less excited' prisoners stepped in; then stripped and scrubbed him.

framing.detail: Wire opened 'Judge Lynch came very near making an end of Umphreys' and called him 'The brute'; headlines 'Almost Lynched by Fellow Prisoners', 'Almost Lynched in Jail', 'A Narrow Escape'.
The San Antonio Daily Light headed the wire 'Too Much Mercy for Him'.
The Washington Critic headed its version 'Tender-Hearted Jail Birds'.
The New York Sun ('Judge Lynch in Prison') replaced 'The brute' with 'The man'; Lancaster used his name.
Maysville Evening Bulletin: 'A Negro Rapist's Narrow Escape', calling him 'the colored brute' and 'wretch' while describing him as 'the victim' who pleaded for his life.
Ohio Democrat headlines: 'Rough Usage. Indignant Prisoners Handle a Rapist Without Gloves.'

conflicts.note: The versions can be partly reconciled (prisoners ended the hanging, officials came later), but only the fuller account says the abuse resumed.
All versions place the jailing and attack on Wednesday, May 16.
The fuller account gives the full name twice.
